question: You have opened the disconnects, verified the blades open, released stored energy, and applied locks. Under NFPA 70E-2024 120.6, what comes next, before anyone grounds the conductors?
choices: Apply temporary protective grounds immediately so the bus cannot float
Test each phase conductor phase-to-phase and phase-to-ground for absence of voltage, proving the instrument before and after
Reclose the control power to see whether the lock holds
Remove the locks, test, then reapply the locks
explanation: 120.6 step 7 is the absence-of-voltage test with a before-and-after instrument check. Grounding, when induced or stored energy is a concern, is step 8 and follows that test. Grounds are not a substitute for the test.

question: A worker will be inside the limited approach boundary of exposed 480 V parts. What does NFPA 70E-2024 110.2(B) require before the work?
choices: An energized work permit only, because 480 V is below 1000 V
The conductors put into an electrically safe work condition, unless a listed exception applies
Arc-flash PPE only; shock boundaries start at 1000 V
Nothing, if the worker is a Level II technician
explanation: At 50 V and above, 110.2(B) requires an electrically safe work condition before work inside the limited approach boundary, or before interaction that raises arc-flash likelihood. Exceptions (normal operation, opening a disconnect to create the safe condition, infeasibility, additional hazards, and under 50 V with the source considered) are specific. Job title is not one of them.

question: For exposed fixed 480 V AC parts, Table 130.4(E)(a) gives which shock boundaries?
choices: Limited approach 10 ft, restricted approach 3 ft 6 in
Limited approach 5 ft, restricted approach 2 ft 2 in
Limited approach 3 ft 6 in, restricted approach 1 ft 0 in
Limited approach 3 ft 6 in, restricted approach avoid contact
explanation: 480 V phase-to-phase sits in the 151 V–750 V row. For fixed circuit parts the limited approach boundary is 3 ft 6 in and the restricted approach boundary is 1 ft 0 in. Avoid contact is the restricted boundary on the 50 V–150 V row. The 5 ft / 2 ft 2 in pair is the 5.1–15 kV fixed-part row.

question: The arc-flash boundary is the distance at which incident energy equals which value?
choices: 0.5 cal/cm²
1.2 cal/cm²
8 cal/cm²
40 cal/cm²
explanation: Article 100 and 130.5(E)(1) both put the arc-flash boundary where incident energy equals 1.2 cal/cm² (5 J/cm²), the second-degree burn threshold used by the standard. 8 and 40 are clothing or folk limits, not the boundary definition.

question: An unqualified helper needs to cross the limited approach boundary to hold a flashlight. What does 130.4(F)(3) allow?
choices: They may enter alone if they wear the same shirt as the qualified person
A qualified person must explain the hazard and escort them continuously, and they still may not cross the restricted approach boundary
They may cross both the limited and restricted boundaries if voltage is under 1000 V
Unqualified people are banned from the limited approach boundary with no escort exception
explanation: Entry into the limited approach boundary by an unqualified person requires a briefing and a continuous escort by a qualified person. The same paragraph forbids that unqualified person from crossing the restricted approach boundary under any circumstance.

question: You are about to prove a 480 V starter is de-energized. What does 110.6(E) require of the test instrument?
choices: A calibration sticker dated within 12 months is enough; no live check is required
Verify it on a known voltage source before the absence-of-voltage test and again after
Verify it only after the test, so you do not expose yourself twice
Use any proximity tester; contact instruments are banned under 1000 V
explanation: When the circuit is 50 V or more, 110.6(E) requires the instrument to be verified on a known voltage source before and after the absence-of-voltage test. 120.6(7) repeats that check inside the electrically-safe-work-condition sequence.

question: Class 0 rubber insulating gloves, Table 130.7(C)(7)(a), have what maximum AC use voltage?
explanation: Class 00 is 500 V AC, class 0 is 1000 V AC, class 1 is 7500 V AC, class 2 is 17000 V AC. A 480 V test still needs a class whose AC rating covers the exposure, and protectors, unless the narrow no-protector exception is met.

question: How often does Table 130.7(C)(7)(b) require rubber insulating gloves to be electrically retested after they are issued?
choices: Every 6 months
Every 12 months
Every 24 months
Only when they fail an air test
explanation: Gloves: before first issue and every 6 months thereafter. Blankets and sleeves in the same table are every 12 months. The air test is the daily inspection in 130.7(C)(7)(c), not a substitute for the electrical retest interval.

question: NFPA 70E-2024 110.2(A) says the electrically safe work condition policy must put which risk-control idea first?
choices: PPE category selection
Hazard elimination
Arc-flash labeling
A written variance for every test
explanation: 110.2(A)(1) requires hazard elimination to be the first priority when safety-related work practices are implemented. PPE is what you use when the hazard is not yet eliminated. The informational note points at elimination as the first method in the hierarchy in 110.3(H).

question: A qualified person will troubleshoot a live 480 V control circuit inside the restricted approach boundary, with the required PPE and practices. Which statement matches 130.2?
choices: An energized electrical work permit is always required inside the restricted approach boundary, including troubleshooting
Troubleshooting and voltage measuring by a qualified person using the required practices and PPE may proceed without an energized electrical work permit
Permits are required only above 1000 V
Thermography that crosses the restricted approach boundary is exempt, but voltage testing is not
explanation: 130.2(A) requires a permit for work inside the restricted approach boundary. 130.2(C)(1) exempts testing, troubleshooting, and voltage measuring when a qualified person uses the Chapter 1 practices and PPE. Thermography is exempt only when the restricted approach boundary is not crossed.

question: A label project wants both an incident-energy number and an arc-flash PPE category on the same switchgear section. What does 130.5(F) say?
choices: Both methods are required so the label has a backup
Either the incident-energy method or the PPE-category method may be used on that equipment, not both
The category method is mandatory below 600 V and the incident-energy method above
Incident energy may be converted into a category from Table 130.7(C)(15)(c)
explanation: 130.5(F) allows the incident-energy analysis method or the PPE category method. Either, but not both, on the same piece of equipment. It also forbids using an incident-energy result to specify a category from Table 130.7(C)(15)(c).

question: Which condition means the equipment is not in the normal operating condition described in 110.2(B) Exception No. 1?
choices: Covers are on and secured, and there is no sign of impending failure
The door is open and there is evidence of arcing at the stabs
The gear is used the way the listing and the manufacturer describe
The equipment is rated for the available fault current
explanation: The exception requires doors closed and secured, covers in place, and no evidence of impending failure. Arcing and an open door each break the list. The informational note gives arcing, overheating, loose parts, damage, deterioration, and water as examples of impending failure.

question: A test lead jacket is nicked to the copper. What does 110.6(D) require?
choices: Tape it and finish the outage; replace it next quarter
Remove the damaged lead from service until a person qualified to do the repair makes it safe
Keep using it below 50 V only
Derate the meter one CAT level and continue
explanation: Instruments, leads, probes, and cords are inspected before each use. A defect that could expose someone means the item is removed from service. Nobody uses it until a person qualified for that repair has restored it.

question: OSHA 3120 contrasts a lockout device with a tagout device. Which description matches the booklet?
choices: They provide the same protection; the tag is only a different color
A lock is a positive restraint that takes force or a key to defeat; a tag is a warning and, by itself, protects less
A tag is stronger because more people can read it
Locks are only for mechanical valves, tags are only for electrical breakers
explanation: OSHA 3120 describes lockout devices as positive restraints and tagout devices as prominent warnings that are easier to remove and provide less protection on their own. The electrical sequence you still follow in the field is NFPA 70E-2024 120.6.
reference: OSHA 3120 (2002 rev.), lockout and tagout device descriptions

question: On Table 130.4(E)(a), the restricted approach boundary for fixed exposed parts at 50 V to 150 V is:
choices: 1 ft 0 in
Avoid contact
3 ft 6 in
Not specified
explanation: The 50–150 V row lists a limited approach of 3 ft 6 in for fixed parts and a restricted approach of avoid contact. Not specified is the under-50 V row. 1 ft 0 in is the restricted boundary starting at 151 V.

question: A coworker says a 40 cal/cm² suit means the pressure wave is covered because the PPE category was selected correctly. What does the 130.7 informational note actually limit?
choices: PPE rules are written for shock and the thermal effects of an arc; they do not claim to stop physical trauma from the blast
PPE above 40 cal/cm² is prohibited by 130.7
The note says leather gloves stop both heat and pressure
Incident energy already includes blunt trauma, so no extra judgment is needed
explanation: The note under 130.7 says the PPE requirements address arc flash and shock. Because some arcs explode, physical trauma can still occur, and those requirements do not address trauma other than the thermal exposure. Hazard elimination in 110.2(A) is still first.

question: Class 1 rubber insulating gloves are rated for what maximum AC use voltage in Table 130.7(C)(7)(a)?
explanation: Class 00 is 500 V, class 0 is 1000 V, class 1 is 7500 V, and class 2 is 17000 V AC. The class has to cover the voltage you can actually touch.

question: For fixed exposed AC parts at 5.1 kV to 15 kV, Table 130.4(E)(a) lists the limited and restricted approach boundaries as:
choices: 3 ft 6 in and 1 ft 0 in
5 ft 0 in and 2 ft 2 in
10 ft 0 in and avoid contact
2 ft 1 in and 1 ft 0 in
explanation: Fixed parts in that row are a 5 ft limited approach and a 2 ft 2 in restricted approach. The 3 ft 6 in / 1 ft 0 in pair is the 151–750 V row. Do not carry the low-voltage numbers onto a 15 kV termination.

question: Which fiber is forbidden in underlayers next to skin when arc-rated clothing is required?
choices: Cotton
Wool
Polyester
A nonmelting fabric used only as an outer shell
explanation: 130.7 bars meltable underlayers: acetate, nylon, polyester, polypropylene, and spandex. Cotton and wool are the usual nonmelting layers. An outer shell is a different rule.

question: Before the first use of the day, rubber insulating gloves are:
choices: Electrically retested in the shop every morning
Air-tested along with the visual inspection
Wetted so they seal to the hand
Legal to use with a cut if the cuff is rolled
explanation: 130.7(C)(7)(c) pairs the daily inspection with an air test. The electrical retest interval is six months in Table 130.7(C)(7)(b), not every morning.

question: High-capacitance elements, before the associated equipment is touched, are to be:
choices: Left charged so the megger reading stays stable
Discharged, then shorted and grounded
Only tagged, because a capacitor cannot reclose a breaker
Tested with a proximity pen and then ignored
explanation: 120.5(B)(2) says capacitors are discharged and high-capacitance elements are also short-circuited and grounded. A tag does not bleed the charge.

question: Thermography that stays outside the restricted approach boundary, done by a qualified person with the required PPE, is:
choices: Always a permit job
One of the energized-work-permit exemptions
Forbidden above 50 V
A substitute for an absence-of-voltage test
explanation: 130.2(C)(2) exempts thermography, ultrasound, and visual inspection when the restricted approach boundary is not crossed. Crossing that boundary, or opening gear into the boundary, puts the exemption away.

question: A 480 V meter and its leads must be:
choices: Any CAT II meter, because the panel is indoors
Rated for the circuit, approved for the use, and used as the maker instructs
Rated only for the control voltage
Replaced by a solenoid tester with no category mark
explanation: 110.6(B) requires the instrument and its accessories to be rated for where they are used, approved for the purpose, and used to the instructions. The location’s category still has to match the meter.

question: The arc-flash boundary and the limited approach boundary are:
choices: Always the same distance
Independent; the arc-flash boundary can be the farther one
Both taken from Table 130.4(E)(a)
Canceled once an energized work permit is signed
explanation: The note under 130.4(E) says the shock boundaries and the arc-flash boundary are independent, and the arc-flash boundary can be farther out. Table 130.4(E)(a) is shock only; 130.5(E) is the arc-flash boundary.

question: Class 4 rubber gloves, Table 130.7(C)(7)(a), maximum AC use voltage is:
explanation: Class 3 is 26500 V and class 4 is 36000 V AC. The DC column is higher and is not the number you quote for an AC line.

question: Rubber gloves used without leather protectors, under the narrow exception, have their AC class:
choices: Left unchanged
Reduced by half for class 00, and by one whole class for classes 0 through 4
Raised one class
Limited to control wiring only
explanation: 130.7(C)(7)(a) allows bare rubber only with no cutting risk, a retest before the gloves are used again, and that voltage derating. The six-month electrical test still exists for gloves that stay in service with protectors.

question: An incident-energy analysis is reviewed:
choices: Only after a fault
At intervals not exceeding 5 years, and sooner if the system changes
Every outage
When the PPE category table is also applied to the same equipment
explanation: 130.5(G) says the analysis is updated when distribution changes could affect it, and reviewed at intervals not to exceed 5 years. 130.5(F) still forbids pairing that analysis with a PPE category on the same equipment.

question: Before a contract crew works, the host employer’s duty in 110.5(A) includes:
choices: Lending them the host’s locks with no briefing
Informing them of known hazards covered by 70E that they might not recognize
Signing their energized work permit after the job
Waiving approach boundaries for testing
explanation: The host tells the contractor about known hazards related to the work and about installation information the contractor needs. The contractor still has to train its own people and follow the standard.

question: Incident energy for PPE selection is based on the distance to the worker’s:
choices: Hands only
Face and chest
Feet
The arc-flash label, whatever distance it prints
explanation: 130.5(G) uses the working distance to the face and chest. Hands closer than that distance need extra protection even when the shirt is rated for the chest. The label does not invent a new distance.

question: Table 130.4(E)(b) for DC, 301 V to 1 kV, restricted approach boundary is:
choices: Avoid contact
1 ft 0 in
3 ft 6 in
5 ft 0 in
explanation: That DC row is a 3 ft 6 in limited approach for fixed parts and a 1 ft 0 in restricted approach. Avoid contact is the 50–300 V DC restricted boundary. Do not paste the AC 15 kV numbers onto a DC bus.

question: Under 29 CFR 1910.147, which of these is an energy-isolating device?
choices: A push button
A selector switch
A disconnect switch that opens all ungrounded conductors
A relay target
explanation: The definition lists breakers, disconnects, and valves. Push buttons, selector switches, and other control-circuit devices are called out as not isolating devices. A tag on a start button does not isolate the circuit.

question: 29 CFR 1910.147 describes a tag, compared with a lock, as:
choices: A physical restraint equal to a lock
A warning device that does not itself hold the isolator
Stronger, because more people can read it
Required only on hydraulic valves
explanation: The training rule says tags are warning devices and do not provide the physical restraint a lock provides. They still may not be ignored or pulled by someone else.

question: 29 CFR 1910.333 says control-circuit devices such as push buttons and interlocks:
choices: May be the only means of de-energizing
May not be the sole means of de-energizing, and interlocks are not a substitute for lockout
Replace a qualified person’s voltage test
Are energy-isolating devices
explanation: The circuits to be worked on are disconnected from all sources. Control devices cannot be the only step, and an interlock is not lockout. Then the absence of voltage is still proved.

question: Conductors that have been switched off but not locked or tagged are treated by 29 CFR 1910.333 as:
choices: De-energized and safe to touch
Energized parts
Exempt below 1000 V
Safe if a second person watches
explanation: Paragraph (b)(1) says parts that are de-energized but not locked or tagged under that section are treated as energized. Off is not the same as isolated.

question: Before a test instrument is used, 29 CFR 1910.334 requires:
choices: A yearly laboratory hipot only
A visual inspection of the instrument, leads, probes, and connectors, and removal from service if damaged
That the leads be wrapped in tape if nicked
No inspection if the meter is CAT III
explanation: Damaged instruments and leads come out of service until repaired and tested. A category rating does not excuse a cut lead.

question: Before circuits are re-energized, 29 CFR 1910.333 requires a qualified person to verify that:
choices: The locks stay on
Tools, jumpers, shorts, and grounds have been removed
The tag may stay as a spare
Only the control power is off
explanation: Paragraph (b)(2)(v) is the return-to-service check: tools, jumpers, shorts, and grounds come off, then people are clear, then locks come off by the people who hung them. Leaving a ground set on and closing in is a fault.

question: An electrical safety interlock may be defeated, under 29 CFR 1910.333, only when:
choices: Anyone needs a faster test
A qualified person does it temporarily while working, and puts the interlock back when finished
The tagout is in place, so the interlock is redundant forever
The door is closed
explanation: Only a qualified person, only while the work is in progress, and the interlock is returned to service. A defeated door switch left that way is how the next person gets hurt.

question: For a circuit over 600 V nominal, 29 CFR 1910.333 requires the test instrument used to prove de-energized to be checked:
choices: Once a year
Immediately before and immediately after the test
Only after the test
Only if it is a proximity tester
explanation: Paragraph (b)(2)(iv)(B) adds the before-and-after check specifically when the circuit is over 600 V. NFPA 70E’s before-and-after rule starts at 50 V. Know which document you are standing under.

question: 29 CFR 1910.269 does not apply to:
choices: Generation, transmission, and distribution work covered in that section
Electrical installations and work practices covered by subpart S
Line-clearance tree trimming done by qualified employees for the utility
Work on transmission lines
explanation: 1910.269(a)(1)(ii)(B) carves out subpart S installations. A plant distribution system maintained under subpart S is not automatically a 1910.269 job. Generation and transmission work that the section does cover still is.

question: Work on circuit parts that have not been de-energized under 29 CFR 1910.333(b) may be done by:
choices: Any employee wearing gloves
Only a qualified person, familiar with the practices, PPE, and insulated tools
A helper if a qualified person is on site but not at the point of work
Anyone, below 480 V
explanation: 1910.333(c)(2) limits that work to qualified persons who can work the circuit safely and know the PPE, shielding, and tools. Being nearby is not the same as being the qualified person at the work.

question: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 says, about its own safety coverage:
choices: It replaces OSHA and NFPA 70E for acceptance testing
It does not claim to cover every safety issue, so the user still has to check the regulations that apply
It is only a lockout procedure
It forbids any test above 50 V
explanation: Section 1 says the work can involve hazardous voltages and that the specifications do not purport to address every safety issue. The user reviews the applicable regulations. ATS is the test specification, not the safety manual.

question: ATS-2025 section 3.2 requires the on-site crew leader to hold:
choices: Any helper card
A current ANSI/NETA ETT certification of Level 3 or higher
Only an OSHA 10 card
A manufacturer’s relay-software login
explanation: Technicians are certified under ANSI/NETA ETT. The crew leader on site holds a current Level 3 or higher. A software password does not replace that certification.

question: ATS-2025 section 3.2 says the person running the tests must be able to:
choices: Skip the hazard review if the gear is new
Work safely, know the hazards, and judge whether the equipment is fit for service
Sign the report without looking at the data
Test energized parts as the normal method
explanation: The technician is trained on the apparatus, can run the tests safely with a real knowledge of the hazards, and has to judge serviceability from the data. New equipment does not cancel that.

question: Before switchgear is treated as ready for service, ATS 7.1.1 says to confirm that:
choices: Shipping bracing, loose parts, and papers shipped inside the cubicles are still packed in place
Shipping bracing, loose parts, and documentation shipped inside cubicles have been removed
The mimic bus has been painted over
The shutters are tied open
explanation: Visual inspection includes a clean unit with shipping bracing, loose parts, and shipped paperwork removed. Leaving a brace in a cubicle is how a new lineup is damaged on the first close.

question: Before acceptance testing starts, ATS-2025 section 4.1 says the owner’s representative provides:
choices: Only the transformer oil sample
Site-specific hazard notification and safety training
A waiver of lockout
The test set’s calibration sticker
explanation: The owner also supplies studies, drawings, and notice of when the gear is available. The hazard notification and the site safety training are the owner’s item in that list, not something the test crew invents after the first shock.

question: ATS 7.1.1.D.2 says a dielectric withstand on switchgear bus:
choices: Comes before the insulation-resistance test, to save time
Does not proceed until insulation resistance is above the minimum
Replaces the insulation-resistance test
Is optional whenever the gear is indoor
explanation: Insulation resistance is compared with the manufacturer or with Table 100.1. Withstand waits until that resistance is high enough. A low reading is investigated, not hipot’d through.

question: ATS 7.1.1.A.10 proves a switchgear interlock by:
choices: Defeating the interlock and leaving it defeated
Trying to close a locked-open device, trying to open a locked-closed device, and exchanging keys through the scheme
Removing the locks so the test is faster
Operating the breaker from the relay test set only
explanation: The inspection tries the blocked operations and walks the key exchange with every device in the scheme. That is a test of the interlock, not permission to bypass it. OSHA still treats a defeated interlock as temporary and qualified-person work, and it has to be restored.

question: ATS 7.1.1.A.13 requires shutters and barriers in switchgear to be:
choices: Removed for the life of the gear
Installed and operating correctly
Replaced with cardboard
Checked only if someone is shocked
explanation: Shutters cover the primary stabs when a breaker is withdrawn. A shutter tied open is a live-part exposure the inspection is supposed to catch before the lineup is called accepted.

question: ATS 7.1.1.A.6 says fuse and breaker sizes in a lineup must agree with:
choices: Whatever is on the truck
The drawings and the coordination study
The largest frame that fits
The relay firmware version only
explanation: The device that is installed has to be the device the study used. A larger fuse than the study can leave the downstream cable unprotected. The microprocessor breaker address is checked at the same time.

question: ATS 7.1.1.A.16 checks filters and vents so that:
choices: The gear can be painted
Cooling paths are actually open
The insulation-resistance test can be skipped
Shipping braces can stay in
explanation: A plugged vent is a thermal problem waiting for load. The inspection confirms filters are in place and vents are clear. It does not replace the insulation test.

question: Trying to close a locked-open breaker during an ATS 7.1.1 interlock check is:
choices: A permanent defeat of the interlock
The way you prove the interlock holds
A substitute for lockout
Required only on low-voltage panelboards
explanation: The attempt should fail. If the breaker closes, the interlock does not provide the protection the drawing claims. That is different from a qualified person temporarily defeating an interlock under 29 CFR 1910.333(c)(10), which has to be put back.

question: During the VLF withstand in ATS 7.3.3.B.5.2, shields and conductors not under test are:
choices: Left floating
Grounded
Tied to the test lead
Removed from the terminations
explanation: The conductor or conductors under test are energized. Everything else, shields included, is grounded. A floating shield is a shock hazard and it changes the test.

question: ATS 7.1.1.A.1 starts the switchgear inspection by comparing the nameplate with the drawings because:
choices: A wrong voltage class will be tested at the wrong level
The nameplate is optional on new gear
The mimic bus replaces the nameplate
Only the relay settings matter
explanation: Acceptance tests apply voltages taken from the equipment rating. If the nameplate is not the drawing, you may hipot a 5 kV bus at a 15 kV value, or the reverse, and miss a real defect. The comparison comes before the electrical tests.

question: ATS 7.1.1.A.3 includes which mechanical safety checks on switchgear?
choices: Anchorage, alignment, grounding, and required clearances
Only the paint color
Only the relay firmware
The dissolved-gas sample
explanation: A lineup that is not anchored, not aligned, poorly grounded, or short of working clearance is not ready, even if the insulation resistance is high. Those four items are in the visual inspection.

question: ATS 7.1.1.A.12 tells you to inspect switchgear insulators for:
choices: Physical damage or contaminated surfaces
The correct Duval zone
A polarization index of 2.0
Pilot-wire guard frequency
explanation: Cracked or dirty insulation is a flashover path. The visual check is required. It does not replace the insulation-resistance test that follows.

question: ATS 7.1.1.A.15 requires mechanical indicating devices on switchgear to:
choices: Operate correctly, so open and closed are not a guess
Be removed before energizing
Match the oil color
Be tested only with primary current
explanation: A false open indication is how a disconnect gets approached as de-energized. The indicators are checked in the visual inspection, before anyone relies on them.

question: ATS 7.22.1.B.4 says to functionally test engine shutdown for:
choices: Low oil pressure, overtemperature, and overspeed, among the protections that apply
High power factor only
A loss-of-field relay only
Cable shield resistance
explanation: The section’s note says that, other than protective shutdowns, the prime mover is outside the specification. Those shutdowns are still tested. A generator that will not trip on overspeed is not an accepted emergency set.

question: On panelboards, ATS 7.1.2 says a dielectric withstand:
choices: Waits until insulation resistance is above the minimum
Replaces the insulation-resistance test
Is performed at the VLF cable voltage
Is skipped when the directory is typed
explanation: The panelboard electrical values use the same gate as switchgear. Insulation resistance is compared with the manufacturer or with Table 100.1, and withstand does not go forward while that reading is still low.

question: After a machine insulation-resistance test, IEEE 43-2013 clause 5.5 requires:
choices: Leave the winding charged so the next reading is faster
A discharge path once the test voltage is removed
A second test at twice the voltage immediately
No discharge, because the current is already zero
explanation: The winding holds the charge. Clause 5.5 says to provide a discharge circuit after the direct voltage comes off. ATS 7.15.1 runs this test in accordance with IEEE 43. Pulling the leads first is how people get hit.

question: IEEE C57.13.1-2017 clause 12.1 says a current transformer must not be left energized above the knee:
choices: For the whole lunch break, so the curve can settle
Any longer than it takes to record the points
Until the primary is reconnected to the bus
At rated primary current for 30 minutes
explanation: Voltage on part of the secondary induces voltage on the whole winding. Clause 12.1 says not to stay above the knee longer than the readings require, and to demagnetize a de-energized CT before the run. ATS 7.10.1.B.4 is the excitation test this clause is describing.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.4; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clause 12.1

question: IEEE 43-2013 clause 5.3 warns that an insulation-resistance test voltage that is too high:
choices: Always gives a better PI
Can overstress the insulation and fail it, especially on a small, low-voltage, or wet winding
Is required above 1000 V by Table 1 with no upper bound
Replaces the discharge step
explanation: The test is a direct-voltage test. Table 1 is a guide, and the manufacturer’s limit still wins. ATS Table 100.11 uses the same idea: the test voltage follows the winding rating. Do not pick the top of the meter.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.11 and 7.15.1.B.2; ref. IEEE 43-2013, clause 5.3

question: NFPA 70B-2026 limits a retorque check on threaded hardware that is already installed to:
choices: 100 percent of the original torque, plus a quarter turn
No more than 90 percent of the manufacturer’s original specified torque
50 percent, so the bolt cannot yield
Whatever a click wrench happens to read
explanation: The 90 percent cap is for hardware that was torqued before. Going back to the full original value on a joint that has already been tightened can damage the bolt or the lug. If the manufacturer published no number, the applicable fastener table is the fallback, and metric hardware stays with the manufacturer.

question: A brand-new threaded electrical connection, under NFPA 70B-2026, is tightened to:
choices: 90 percent of the table, the same as a retorque
The manufacturer’s specified torque, or the applicable table if the manufacturer is silent
Finger tight, because the inspection is infrared
Half the bolt diameter in inch-pounds, always
explanation: The 90 percent limit is the retorque rule for hardware that is already in service. A new joint gets the full specified torque. Do not mix the two.

question: For equipment rated through 1000 V, NFPA 70B-2026 calls for insulation resistance as:
choices: A DC test that does not exceed the manufacturer’s test voltage
An AC hipot at twice rated voltage for one minute
A very-low-frequency test at a medium-voltage table
Whatever the meter’s top range is
explanation: Through 1000 V the method is DC insulation resistance, with a calibrated instrument, and the voltage stays at or below the manufacturer’s test voltage. If the manufacturer is silent, an industry standard is the next stop. These chapters do not publish a polarization-index or dielectric-absorption limit.

question: Before field tests, NFPA 70B-2026 says to assess special hazards such as:
choices: Only the paint color
Stored energy, insulating gas, PCBs, asbestos, and similar listed hazards
The brand of the torque wrench only
Whether the one-line uses device numbers
explanation: The list includes overpotential sources, stored or mass energy, gas byproducts and electrolytes, asbestos, insulating gas, PCBs, and tetrachloroethylene. The test does not start until those are accounted for.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 requires test instruments to be:
choices: Any meter that turns on
Sound, used as the manufacturer says, calibrated, and rated for the task
Calibrated once in the life of the company
Rated only if the circuit is over 1000 V
explanation: Calibration information has to be easy to find, and the interval has to fit how accurate the instrument must be and how it is used. A meter that is not rated for the voltage is not made acceptable by a fresh sticker.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 Table 9.3.2 treats visual inspection and cleaning of portable tools as:
choices: Once a year
Before each use
Every 60 months
Only after a shock
explanation: Visual inspection and cleaning are before each use. Electrical testing of those tools is on a 3-month interval in every condition column. That is tighter than the ordinary equipment row.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 classes 1, 1A, 2, and 2A are:
choices: Online standard, online enhanced, offline standard, and offline enhanced
Four torque tables
Polarization index, dielectric absorption, tip-up, and tan delta
Condition numbers 1 through 4
explanation: Online means the equipment is connected to its supply. Offline means it is disconnected or fed from a test source. Enhanced means the test gathers extra diagnostic information. It is not a different kind of equipment.

question: Under NFPA 70B-2026, how are a harsh environment and criticality brought into the condition score?
choices: A harsh environment is condition 3 when the equipment is not rated or evaluated for it, and criticality follows reliability and continuity concerns
Environment and criticality are averaged with the physical score
A harsh site stays condition 1 as long as the gear is energized
Criticality is scored from how new the paint is
explanation: A harsh environment puts the equipment in condition 3 when it was not specifically rated or evaluated for that environment. Criticality is assigned from reliability and continuity concerns, not from appearance. Those two factors are how the environment and the importance of the equipment enter the score.

question: When an interval is taken from NFPA 70B-2026, the first place to look is:
choices: The table, even when the manufacturer published a shorter interval

The manufacturer's instructions first. The table's fit also depends on whether predictive methods are available, and a longer interval needs a written justification after more than two problem-free intervals
Always 12 months
The last technician's preference, with nothing written down
explanation: Manufacturer instructions come first. The table is not used only because the manufacturer was silent. Whether it applies also depends on whether predictive methods are available. An interval longer than the table needs a documented justification, and that extension is allowed after more than two intervals without problems.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 allows an undisturbed bolted bus joint to be assessed by:
choices: Torque only, and never by infrared or resistance
One or more of infrared, permanently mounted temperature sensors, contact resistance, or torque verification
A polarization index of the bus
A visual look with no instrument
explanation: Any one of those methods can be the assessment, and more than one is allowed. Contact-resistance readings above the manufacturer’s maximum are investigated. A retorque, if you use one, still stops at 90 percent of the original torque.

question: For equipment rated above 1000 V, NFPA 70B-2026 says the insulation test method is:
choices: Always a DC megohmmeter, same as equipment through 1000 V
Chosen by the electrical maintenance program from the methods that section lists
Always a 60-minute power-frequency withstand
Left to whoever is holding the meter
explanation: Above 1000 V the program selects among DC insulation resistance, AC or DC withstand, DC overpotential, power factor or dissipation factor, very low frequency, damped AC, acoustic ultrasonic, and partial discharge. Through 1000 V, the specified method is DC insulation resistance. These chapters still do not publish a polarization-index limit.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 says equipment with an impending failure that threatens people, health, or the environment is:
choices: Left in service until the next scheduled interval
De-energized and designated nonserviceable, unless that would add hazards or raise the risk, or it cannot be done
Tagged limited-service and kept loaded
Repaired only if the condition score is 1
explanation: The usual step is to de-energize the equipment and mark it nonserviceable. The exception is wider than one greater hazard: it covers additional hazards or an increase in risk, and the case where de-energizing cannot be done. Barricades and alerts stay in place until the equipment is de-energized or repaired. Limited-service is not the label for a failure that is about to hurt someone.

question: A contact-resistance reading on an undisturbed bolted joint that is above the manufacturer’s maximum is, under NFPA 70B-2026:
choices: Accepted if it was retorqued to 100 percent
Investigated
Ignored when an infrared camera is on site
Converted to a polarization index
explanation: The joint is assessed by infrared, a permanent sensor, contact resistance, or torque, alone or together. A resistance above the manufacturer’s maximum is not left as a number on the sheet. A retorque of that existing hardware still does not exceed 90 percent of the original torque.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 condition 1 means the equipment is:
choices: Like new: clean, tight, dry, maintenance current, and no open monitoring items or recommendations
Any gear that is still energized
Gear that missed the last two maintenance cycles
Gear that needs a major part replaced this cycle
explanation: Condition 1 is the clean case: maintenance is current, and there are no open monitoring items or recommendations. Condition 2 keeps only some of those condition-1 criteria, not the whole set, and it carries at least one concern. Condition 3 is the step where operation has changed, maintenance cycles were missed, or an alarm is still unaddressed.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 puts equipment in condition 3 when, among other triggers:
choices: The enclosure was wiped down
The last two maintenance cycles were missed, or both of the previous cycles needed a major repair or replacement
One infrared scan was normal
The manufacturer interval is longer than the table
explanation: Other triggers are an operating change, an unaddressed monitoring notification, or an urgent action. Two missed cycles are enough by themselves. Condition 2 is the milder step, where the basics are still met and only one concern has shown up.

question: NFPA 70E-2024 requires a documented energized work permit when work is performed inside which boundary?
choices: The limited approach boundary, by itself
The restricted approach boundary
The arc-flash boundary only, with no shock boundary involved
Any distance inside the equipment room
explanation: 130.2(A)(1) requires the permit for work inside the restricted approach boundary. A second case is interaction with equipment when an arc-flash injury is more likely even though parts are not exposed. Simply being inside the limited approach boundary is not that first line. Testing and troubleshooting by a qualified person using the required practices can be exempt under 130.2(C).

question: On a 480 V system, which statement matches NFPA 70E-2024 Table 130.4(E)(a) for fixed exposed parts?
choices: Limited approach 1 ft, restricted approach 3 ft 6 in
Limited approach 3 ft 6 in, restricted approach 1 ft
Both boundaries are 10 ft
There is no restricted boundary below 1000 V
explanation: 151 V to 750 V fixed parts: limited approach 3 ft 6 in, restricted approach 1 ft. The permit in 130.2 is tied to the restricted boundary, not to the limited boundary. An unqualified person does not cross the restricted boundary.

question: Rubber insulating gloves for work at 13.8 kV AC, using the maximum-use voltages in NFPA 70E-2024 Table 130.7(C)(7)(a), must be at least:
choices: Class 0
Class 1
Class 2
Class 00
explanation: Class 1 is 7,500 V maximum use. Class 2 is 17,000 V. 13.8 kV is above class 1 and within class 2. Class 0 stops at 1,000 V. The glove still needs a leather protector and a current electrical test.

question: A one-line symbol for a surge arrester is defined in:
choices: ATS Table 100.1
IEEE 315 graphic symbols
NFPA 70E Table 130.4(E)(a)
The glove voltage table
explanation: The recalled topic is a drawing symbol. IEEE 315 is on the NETA reference list and defines the one-line symbol for a surge arrester. Do not memorize a forum sketch as the answer. On a job, use the project legend.

question: Under 29 CFR 1910.146, a confined space is permit-required when it has:
choices: Limited entry only, with no atmospheric, engulfment, or configuration hazard
At least one of: a hazardous atmosphere or the potential for one, an engulfment hazard, a trapping configuration, or another recognized serious hazard
A door that a forklift can drive through
Continuous occupancy by design
explanation: A confined space is big enough to enter, has limited entry or exit, and is not meant for continuous occupancy. It is permit-required if any one of the four characteristics is present: hazardous atmosphere (or the potential for one), a material that can engulf a person, walls or a floor that can trap or asphyxiate, or any other recognized serious safety or health hazard. Entry begins when any part of the body breaks the plane of the opening.
reference: 29 CFR 1910.146(b), definitions of confined space and permit-required confined space

question: Hissing and a sweet smell at switchgear are recalled as corona and ozone. The checked action is:
choices: Open the door and sniff to confirm ozone
Treat it as a possible energized hazard and establish an electrically safe condition before a close inspection
Raise the VLF voltage
Ignore it if the mimic is correct
explanation: Hissing and a sweet smell can be corona making ozone. That diagnosis is field fundamentals, not a numbered 70E rule. Treat the condition as a possible energized hazard and establish an electrically safe work condition before a close inspection. Do not open the door to sniff it.

question: In the NFPA 70B-2026 test classes, class 1 and class 2 differ because:
choices: Class 1 is online and connected to the supply; class 2 is offline, disconnected or fed by a test source
Class 1 is always a dissolved-gas test
Class 2 is the only class allowed above 1000 V
The numbers are torque tables
explanation: Online means the equipment is still connected to its supply. Offline means it is disconnected or energized from test equipment. The A suffix, 1A and 2A, means an enhanced test that gathers extra diagnostic information. Thermography under load is an online inspection. A breaker overpotential test is offline.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 marks which of these as an enhanced test rather than the basic insulation-resistance test?
choices: Overpotential on a medium-voltage breaker power circuit, and dielectric withstand on switchgear above 1000 V
Specific gravity of every flooded cell
A visual check that the enclosure is clean
Recording float voltage to two decimals
explanation: Overpotential on a medium-voltage breaker power circuit, and dielectric withstand on switchgear above 1000 V, are enhanced tests rather than the basic insulation-resistance test. The caution about solid-state parts belongs to an overpotential test of control wiring, not to the power-circuit test. The chapters do not print a pass/fail kilovolt for those enhanced tests.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 Table 12.3.5 for switchgear includes ground resistance, bonding, insulation resistance, and protective tests. Above 1000 V it also offers:
choices: Enhanced dielectric withstand and online partial discharge
A required dissolved-gas sample of the bus
Specific gravity of the switchgear
A turns-ratio test of the enclosure
explanation: Those two are the extra choices once the gear is above 1000 V. Online partial discharge is an online test. The withstand test is not performed while the gear is in service. The chapter does not print the withstand kilovolt.

question: Which test is listed for a panelboard in NFPA 70B-2026 Table 13.3.5?
choices: Main-bus insulation resistance, and an enhanced insulation-resistance test of control wiring
Vacuum integrity of a 15 kV bottle
Dissolved gas in the panel oil
Fall-of-potential of the service ground rod as the only panel test
explanation: Panelboards and switchboards in this chapter are 1000 V and below. The electrical list is main-bus insulation resistance, enhanced control-wiring insulation resistance, protective devices, an operational test, and metering. Vacuum integrity and dissolved gas are other chapters.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 visual inspection of substations and switchgear, conditions 1, 2, and 3, is:
choices: 12, 12, and 6 months
60, 36, and 12 months for every switchgear task, including infrared
12, 6, and 3 months
60, 36, and 36 months
explanation: Visual inspection of substations and switchgear is 12, 12, and 6 months. Many other switchgear tasks use 60, 36, and 12 months when the manufacturer is silent, but that row is not every task. Infrared thermography has its own row, and it applies to this equipment too. Above 1000 V the electrical list can add enhanced dielectric withstand and online partial discharge. Those additions do not change the visual interval.

question: Online partial discharge on switchgear above 1000 V, in NFPA 70B-2026, is:
choices: An online test, done while the gear is connected to its supply
An offline overpotential test of control wiring tied to solid-state parts
A specific-gravity test
Required on every panelboard
explanation: Online means the equipment stays connected to the supply. Partial discharge in that switchgear table is the online option. Dielectric withstand is not done on a live bus. Panelboards at 1000 V and below are a different chapter and do not pick up this option just because they are in the same room.

question: Panelboards and switchboards in NFPA 70B-2026, when the manufacturer is silent, are maintained on:
choices: 60, 36, and 12 months
12, 6, and 3 months
The grounding electrical row of 60, 36, and 36 months
12, 12, and 1 month
explanation: That is the standard row for this 1000 V and below equipment. The electrical list is main-bus insulation resistance, an enhanced control-wiring insulation test, protective devices, an operational test, and metering. It is not vacuum integrity and it is not a fluid sample.
